chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Absolute and relative refractive index
question: The absolute refractive indices of media P and Q are 1.8 and 1.2, respectively. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The refractive index of Q relative to P is 1.5.
The refractive index of P relative to Q is 0.67.
The speed of light in P is greater than that in Q.
The refractive index of P relative to Q is 1.5, and light travels more slowly in P.

explanation:
n_{PQ}=(n_P / n_Q)
=(1.8 / 1.2)=1.5


Since v=c/n, light travels more slowly in P. Option A reverses the relative refractive-index ratio.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Why does a ray incident normally suffer no deviation?
question: A ray enters a rectangular glass slab normally. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Glass has the same refractive index as air at normal incidence.
The ray has zero angle of incidence, so Snell's law gives zero angle of refraction, although speed and wavelength change.
Normal incidence prevents the speed of light from changing.
The ray undergoes total internal reflection at both surfaces.

explanation:
is correct?

A) Glass has the same refractive index as air at normal incidence.

B) The ray has zero angle of incidence, so Snell's law gives zero angle of refraction, although speed and wavelength change.

C) Normal incidence prevents the speed of light from changing.

D) The ray undergoes total internal reflection at both surfaces.

**Correct Answer: B**

**Reason:** At normal incidence, i=0^°. Snell's law gives r=0^°, so there is no directional deviation. The ray still travels more slowly in glass and has a shorter wavelength.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Rectangular glass slab
question: Which statement about a ray passing through a parallel-sided glass slab surrounded by air is correct?

options.text: The emergent ray is generally parallel to the incident ray but may be laterally displaced.
The emergent ray is always perpendicular to the incident ray.
The emergent ray is always coincident with the incident ray, irrespective of incidence angle and slab thickness.
The emergent ray must travel towards the normal at the second surface.

explanation: The two slab surfaces are parallel. The angular deviation at the first surface is cancelled by the opposite deviation at the second surface. A lateral displacement generally remains for oblique incidence.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Factors affecting lateral displacement
question: For a fixed refractive index and fixed angle of incidence, what happens to the lateral displacement through a parallel-sided glass slab when its thickness is doubled?

options.text: It becomes half.
It remains unchanged.
It becomes twice as large.
It becomes four times as large.

explanation:
The lateral displacement is


d=t(sin(i-r) / cos r)


For fixed i and r, displacement is directly proportional to slab thickness t. Doubling the thickness doubles the displacement.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Apparent depth
question: An object is viewed vertically from air through a transparent liquid. Which statement is correct for near-normal viewing?

options.text: Apparent depth is always greater than real depth.
Apparent depth is equal to real depth multiplied by the refractive index.
Apparent depth is independent of the refractive index.
Apparent depth equals real depth divided by the refractive index of the liquid relative to air.

concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Apparent shift
question: Which change increases the apparent upward shift of an object viewed normally from air through a liquid, assuming the real depth remains fixed?

options.text: Increasing the refractive index of the liquid.
Decreasing the refractive index of the liquid towards 1.
Reducing the real depth to zero.
Making the refractive index of the liquid equal to that of air.

explanation:
Shift=d_{real}≤ft(1-frac1nright)


For fixed real depth, increasing n increases the apparent shift. When n=1, there is no apparent shift.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Refraction from denser to rarer medium
question: A ray travels from glass into air at an incidence angle smaller than the critical angle. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Total internal reflection must occur because glass is denser.
The ray refracts into air, bending away from the normal.
The ray bends towards the normal because its speed increases.
The ray cannot cross the boundary unless the incidence angle is 90^°.

explanation: When light travels from glass to air below the critical angle, it refracts into air and bends away from the normal. Total internal reflection requires an incidence angle greater than the critical angle, not merely a denser incident medium.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Critical angle
question: Which statement correctly defines the critical angle?

options.text: The angle between the incident ray and the surface when the refracted ray is normal to the surface.
The angle of refraction when the incident angle is 90^°.
The angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is 90^°.
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal during ordinary reflection.

explanation: At the critical angle, the refracted ray travels along the interface. Its angle with the normal is 90^°. The critical angle itself is measured inside the denser medium.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Conditions for total internal reflection
question: Which combination is necessary for total internal reflection at a boundary?

options.text: Light travels from a rarer to a denser medium at any angle.
Light travels from a denser to a rarer medium, but its incidence angle is below the critical angle.
Light travels normally from glass into air.
Light travels from an optically denser to an optically rarer medium, with incidence angle greater than the critical angle.

explanation: Both conditions are necessary: light must approach the boundary from the optically denser medium, and the incidence angle must exceed the critical angle. Neither condition alone is sufficient.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Refractive index and critical angle
question: Two transparent media are surrounded by air. Medium P has a critical angle of 30^°, while medium Q has a critical angle of 45^°. Which statement is correct?

options.text: P has a higher refractive index than Q.
Q has a higher refractive index than P.
Both have equal refractive indices because both critical rays travel along the boundary.
The refractive index cannot be compared using critical angles.

explanation:
n=frac1{sin C}


A smaller critical angle corresponds to a higher refractive index when the surrounding medium is the same. Therefore, P has the higher refractive index.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Optical fibres
question: Why does a conventional optical fibre have a core of higher refractive index than its cladding?

options.text: To make the frequency of light increase in the core.
To ensure light travels faster in the core than in the cladding.
To permit total internal reflection at the core–cladding interface for suitable internal incidence angles.
To prevent the wavelength from changing when light enters the core.

explanation: A higher-index core surrounded by lower-index cladding permits total internal reflection when the internal incidence angle exceeds the critical angle. This guides light along the fibre.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Right-angled prism
question: A right-angled isosceles glass prism is used to deviate a ray through 90^° by total internal reflection. Which condition is essential at the reflecting face?

options.text: The ray must strike the face normally.
The internal angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle for the glass–surrounding-medium pair.
The prism must have a refractive index equal to 1.
The ray must enter the prism from air at 90^° to the surface.

explanation: The ray must undergo total internal reflection at the reflecting face. Therefore, the internal incidence angle must exceed the critical angle, and the surrounding medium must be optically rarer than the prism.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Sparkling of diamonds
question: Which property contributes most directly to the repeated total internal reflections responsible for the brilliance of a properly cut diamond?

options.text: Its refractive index is approximately equal to that of air.
Its critical angle is very large.
Its light absorption is necessarily complete.
Its high refractive index produces a small critical angle.

explanation: Diamond has a refractive index of approximately 2.42, giving a critical angle of about 24.4^° in air. Many rays undergo repeated internal reflection before emerging through suitable facets.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Mirage formation
question: Which explanation best describes a common inferior mirage seen over a hot road?

options.text: Temperature-dependent atmospheric refraction bends rays through layers of varying refractive index, sometimes with total internal reflection contributing to the ray path.
The road produces a real pool of water through condensation.
Light travels in a perfectly straight line through every atmospheric layer.
The phenomenon is caused by the complete absorption of light by hot air.

explanation:
best describes a common inferior mirage seen over a hot road?

A) Temperature-dependent atmospheric refraction bends rays through layers of varying refractive index, sometimes with total internal reflection contributing to the ray path.

B) The road produces a real pool of water through condensation.

C) Light travels in a perfectly straight line through every atmospheric layer.

D) The phenomenon is caused by the complete absorption of light by hot air.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:** Air near the hot road is generally less dense and has a lower refractive index than the cooler air above. The refractive-index gradient bends rays and can produce an apparent image resembling water.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Twinkling of stars
question: Why do stars appear to twinkle?

options.text: Their emitted frequency changes randomly every second.
Atmospheric turbulence continually changes the refraction of their light, causing fluctuations in apparent brightness and position.
Their light undergoes total internal reflection at every atmospheric layer.
Earth's rotation changes the frequency of the light reaching the observer.

explanation: Atmospheric refractive-index variations cause changing ray paths and brightness. Stars appear nearly point-like, making these fluctuations noticeable.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Advanced sunrise and delayed sunset
question: Which statement explains why the Sun can remain visible when its geometric position is slightly below the horizon?

options.text: The atmosphere makes the Sun physically rise earlier.
The atmosphere reflects sunlight only by ordinary mirror reflection.
Atmospheric refraction bends sunlight so that the apparent position of the Sun is higher than its geometric position.
Light travels faster in the lower atmosphere and is therefore accelerated upwards.

explanation: Atmospheric layers have different refractive indices. The curved ray path makes the Sun appear higher than its true geometric position, causing advanced sunrise and delayed sunset.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Refraction and wavelength
question: Which statement about monochromatic light entering glass from air is correct?

options.text: Its speed decreases, its wavelength decreases, and its frequency remains unchanged.
Its speed increases, its wavelength decreases, and its frequency remains unchanged.
Its speed decreases, its frequency increases, and its wavelength remains unchanged.
Its speed and wavelength remain unchanged, but its frequency decreases.

explanation: The refractive index of glass exceeds that of air, so v=c/n decreases. Frequency remains constant at the boundary, and lambda=v/f decreases as well.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Which statement is incorrect?
question: Which statement is incorrect?

options.text: A ray entering a denser medium obliquely generally bends towards the normal.
The refractive index of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in that medium.
The emergent ray from a parallel-sided slab in the same external medium is parallel to the incident ray.
Total internal reflection occurs whenever light crosses from any medium into a medium with a different refractive index.

explanation: Total internal reflection does not occur at every refractive boundary. It requires light to travel from denser to rarer medium with an incidence angle greater than the critical angle.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Matching: Optical phenomenon and explanation
question: Which matching is entirely correct?

options.text: Twinkling of stars — dispersion inside a glass prism.
Advanced sunrise — total internal reflection at the ocean surface.
Apparent depth — backward extensions of refracted rays locate a virtual image closer to the surface.
Diamond brilliance — the frequency of light increases during each internal reflection.

explanation:
Which matching is entirely correct?

A) Twinkling of stars — dispersion inside a glass prism.

B) Advanced sunrise — total internal reflection at the ocean surface.

C) Apparent depth — backward extensions of refracted rays locate a virtual image closer to the surface.

D) Diamond brilliance — the frequency of light increases during each internal reflection.

**Correct Answer: C**

**Reason:** Apparent depth arises because refracted rays entering air are traced backwards to an apparent image. The other options confuse unrelated phenomena or incorrectly describe the physics.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: A ray incident at the critical angle
question: A ray travels from glass into air at exactly the critical angle. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It undergoes total internal reflection with no refracted ray at all.
It refracts towards the normal with angle 0^°.
Its incident angle is 90^°, and its refracted angle is the critical angle.
Its refracted ray travels along the interface, making 90^° with the normal.

explanation: At the critical angle, the refracted angle is 90^°. Total internal reflection occurs only when the incidence angle is greater than the critical angle.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Why a parallel-sided slab does not produce angular deviation
question: Which factor is responsible for the emergent ray being parallel to the incident ray through a rectangular glass slab surrounded by air?

options.text: The refractive index of glass is always exactly 1.5.
The ray undergoes total internal reflection at both slab surfaces.
The opposite angular deviations at the two parallel surfaces cancel.
The incident ray must always be perpendicular to the slab.

explanation: Parallel faces have parallel normals. Refraction at the second surface reverses the angular change introduced at the first, restoring the original direction while generally leaving lateral displacement.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Relative refractive index
question: The refractive index of medium B relative to medium A is less than 1. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Light travels faster in B than in A.
Light must undergo total internal reflection while travelling from A to B.
Medium B must be opaque.
Light travels more slowly in B than in A.

explanation:
For transparent media,


n_{BA}=(v_A / v_B)


If n_{BA}<1, then v_B>v_A. This does not by itself guarantee total internal reflection; the direction and angle of incidence also matter.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Determining whether total internal reflection occurs
question: A ray inside glass of refractive index 1.6 strikes a glass–air boundary at 40^°. What happens at the boundary?

options.text: Total internal reflection occurs because the incidence angle exceeds 30^°.
The ray emerges into air at exactly 90^°.
The ray emerges into air at an angle smaller than 40^°.
The ray refracts into air at an angle greater than 40^° but less than 90^°.

explanation:
The critical angle is


C=sin^{-1}≤ft(frac1{1.6}right)
≈38.7^°


Since 40^°>C, the ray undergoes total internal reflection.

**Correction:** The correct physical conclusion is total internal reflection, so **A should be the correct option**, with the explanation revised to state that the critical angle is approximately 38.7^°.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Time taken by light to cross a glass slab
question: A light ray travels normally through a glass slab 30 cm thick. The refractive index of the glass is 1.5. How long does the ray take to cross the slab?
explanation:
The speed in glass is


v=(3×10^8 / 1.5)
=2×10^8 m/s


The thickness is 0.30 m, so


t=(0.30 / 2×10^8)
=1.5×10^{-9} s


Option D incorrectly uses the speed of light in vacuum.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Finding apparent shift from apparent depth
question: A coin is placed at the bottom of a liquid. Its apparent depth is 16 cm, while the liquid has a refractive index of 1.25. What is the apparent upward shift?

options.text: 4 cm
3.2 cm
20 cm
5 cm

explanation:
First calculate the real depth:


d_{real}=n,d_{app}
=1.25×16=20 cm


Then,


Shift=20-16=4 cm


Option C gives the real depth rather than the shift.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Finding the critical angle from a measured speed
question: Light travels through a transparent material at 2×10^8 m/s. The material is surrounded by air. What is its critical angle?
explanation:
First find the refractive index:


n=(c / v)=(3×10^8 / 2×10^8)=1.5


Then,


sin C=frac1{1.5}=frac23



C≈41.8^°
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Wavelength of light inside glass
question: Monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm in air enters glass of refractive index 1.5. What is its wavelength in glass?

options.text: 900 nm
600 nm
300 nm
400 nm

explanation:
Frequency remains unchanged, so wavelength is inversely proportional to refractive index:


lambda_g=frac{lambda_{air}}{n}
=(600 / 1.5)=400 nm


Option A incorrectly multiplies the wavelength by the refractive index.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Speed and wavelength in a medium
question: Light travels in air at approximately 3×10^8 m/s, with a wavelength of 500 nm. It enters a medium of refractive index 1.25. What are its speed and wavelength in the medium?
explanation:
Speed:


v=(3×10^8 / 1.25)
=2.4×10^8 m/s


Wavelength:


lambda=(500 / 1.25)=400 nm


Frequency remains unchanged. Option B incorrectly assumes the wavelength remains unchanged.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Comparing critical angles in two media
question: The absolute refractive indices of media P and Q are 1.5 and 1.25, respectively. Both are surrounded by air. What is the approximate difference between their critical angles?
explanation:
For P,


C_P=sin^{-1}≤ft(frac1{1.5}right)
≈41.8^°


For Q,


C_Q=sin^{-1}≤ft(frac1{1.25}right)
=sin^{-1}(0.8)≈53.1^°


Difference:


53.1^°-41.8^°=11.3^°


**Correction:** The correct difference is approximately 11.3^°, so none of the options is exact. The closest option is B, 12.0^°, if rounding to the nearest whole-number option is intended.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Apparent depth and apparent shift
question: A coin lies 15 cm below the surface of a liquid of refractive index 1.25. It is viewed nearly normally from air. What are its apparent depth and apparent upward shift?

options.text: 18.75 cm and 3.75 cm
12 cm and 3 cm
12 cm and 15 cm
15 cm and 0 cm

explanation:
d_{apparent}=frac{d_{real}}{n}
=(15 / 1.25)=12 cm


The upward shift is


15-12=3 cm


Option A results from multiplying the real depth by the refractive index.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Relative refractive index and speed ratio
question: The absolute refractive indices of media A and B are 1.2 and 1.5, respectively. What is the refractive index of B relative to A, and how does the speed in B compare with that in A?

options.text: 1.25; speed in B is 1.25 times that in A.
0.80; speed in B is 0.80 times that in A.
1.25; speed in B is 0.80 times that in A.
0.30; speed in B is 0.30 times that in A.

explanation:
Relative refractive index:


n_{BA}=(1.5 / 1.2)=1.25


Since v=c/n,


(v_B / v_A)=(n_A / n_B)
=(1.2 / 1.5)=0.80


The higher-index medium has the lower speed. Option A incorrectly assumes that speed increases with refractive index.
concept_name: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces

title: Predicting whether a ray can emerge from a denser medium

question: A ray strikes a glass–air interface at its critical angle. Which statement correctly distinguishes this situation from total internal reflection?

options.text: The ray undergoes total internal reflection because 45^° exceeds the critical angle.
The ray emerges through the hypotenuse because every prism face permits refraction.
The ray undergoes total internal reflection only if its angle of incidence is 90^°.
The ray bends towards the normal at the hypotenuse and enters air.

explanation: The critical angle for glass–air is approximately 41.8^°. Since 45^°>41.8^°, total internal reflection occurs at the hypotenuse. The ray is reflected internally, changing its direction by 90^°. Option B ignores the critical-angle condition.

question: The light ray repeatedly reflects at the core–cladding interface. An optical fibre has a core of refractive index 1.50 and cladding of refractive index 1.40. Which statement best explains the ray path shown?

options.text: The ray is guided because the core absorbs all the refracted light and re-emits it.
The ray is guided by total internal reflection at the core–cladding interface when the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle for that interface.
The ray is guided because the cladding has a higher refractive index than the core.
The ray is guided because the frequency of light increases at every reflection.

explanation:
The core has the higher refractive index, so light can undergo total internal reflection at the core–cladding interface.


sin C=(1.40 / 1.50)


Thus C≈69^°. For incidence angles inside the core greater than this critical angle, the ray remains guided. Option C reverses the refractive-index relationship.

title: Why does a diamond sparkle intensely?
question: The ray undergoes repeated internal reflections before emerging through a suitable face. A diamond has a very high refractive index, approximately 2.42. Which interpretation of the figure is correct?

options.text: The diamond sparkles because light travels faster inside it than in air.
The diamond sparkles because the frequency of light increases at each internal reflection.
The diamond sparkles because every incident ray undergoes total internal reflection, regardless of its angle.
The diamond can sparkle because its small critical angle allows many rays to undergo repeated total internal reflection before emerging.

explanation:
For diamond–air,


C=sin^{-1}≤ft((1 / 2.42)right)
≈24.4^°


This small critical angle makes total internal reflection possible for many internal rays. Suitable facets then direct light towards the observer. Option C is incorrect because rays incident at angles below the critical angle may refract out instead.

title: Apparent shift of a coin viewed obliquely
question: A submerged object is viewed obliquely from air through a plane water surface. A student views a submerged object obliquely through a horizontal water surface. The student then moves sideways while keeping the eye above the water. Which statement correctly describes the apparent position?

options.text: The apparent image must remain directly above the object for every viewing direction.
The apparent depth is always equal to the real depth because the surface is plane.
The apparent position depends on the viewing direction; the near-normal formula for apparent depth cannot be applied unchanged to every oblique ray.
The object appears deeper because light bends away from the normal when it enters air.

explanation: At a plane interface, the apparent position is determined by tracing the refracted rays backwards. Under near-normal viewing, apparent depth is approximately real depth divided by refractive index. For oblique viewing, the apparent position depends on the ray geometry, so the simple near-normal formula should not be applied indiscriminately. Option D predicts the wrong direction of bending.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Advanced sunrise and delayed sunset
question: Starlight or sunlight bends progressively through atmospheric layers of varying refractive index. The Sun is geometrically just below the horizon, but the observer can still see its apparent image. Which explanation is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 175" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 132 Q80 119 160 132 T312 132" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" /><path d="M8 113 Q80 96 160 113 T312 113" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="4 3" fill="none" /><path d="M8 92 Q80 75 160 92 T312 92" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="4 3" fill="none" /><circle cx="254" cy="142" r="12" fill="#F59E0B" fill-opacity="0.8" /><path d="M254 142 L188 82 L105 47" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M105 47 L70 33" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M77 34 L70 33 L74 40" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><text x="12" y="20" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Observer</text><circle cx="30" cy="30" r="3" fill="currentColor" /><text x="207" y="169" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Geometric horizon</text><text x="17" y="151" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Earth</text><text x="12" y="72" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Atmosphere</text></svg>

options.text: Atmospheric refraction bends sunlight progressively towards regions of higher refractive index, making the Sun appear higher than its geometric position.
The atmosphere reflects all sunlight at the horizon by total internal reflection.
The Sun appears higher because the speed of light increases continuously as it enters denser atmospheric layers.
Atmospheric refraction changes the frequency of sunlight until it becomes visible above the horizon.

explanation:
is correct?

A) Atmospheric refraction bends sunlight progressively towards regions of higher refractive index, making the Sun appear higher than its geometric position.

B) The atmosphere reflects all sunlight at the horizon by total internal reflection.

C) The Sun appears higher because the speed of light increases continuously as it enters denser atmospheric layers.

D) Atmospheric refraction changes the frequency of sunlight until it becomes visible above the horizon.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:**

Atmospheric density and refractive index generally increase closer to Earth's surface. Light curves through the atmosphere, and the backward extension of the final ray places the apparent Sun above its true geometric position. This causes advanced sunrise and delayed sunset. Option B incorrectly attributes the effect to total internal reflection.

title: Twinkling of stars versus the apparent position of planets
question: A point-like star's light passes through turbulent atmospheric layers. Why do stars usually twinkle more noticeably than planets, even though atmospheric refraction affects light from both?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 180" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="30" cy="22" r="5" fill="#F59E0B" /><path d="M30 27 L78 63 L120 90 L167 107 L219 119 L277 126" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M277 126 L294 126" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><circle cx="294" cy="126" r="4" fill="currentColor" /><path d="M10 143 H310" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" /><path d="M65 130 Q75 122 85 130 T105 130 T125 130 T145 130 T165 130 T185 130 T205 130 T225 130 T245 130" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1" fill="none" /><text x="12" y="12" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Star</text><text x="233" y="113" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Observer</text><text x="12" y="161" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Earth's atmosphere</text></svg>

options.text: Stars emit light of changing frequency, whereas planets reflect light of constant frequency.

Stars are point-like sources as seen from Earth, so changing atmospheric refraction causes noticeable fluctuations in their apparent brightness and position; planets have a measurable apparent disc that averages out many fluctuations.
Planets do not undergo atmospheric refraction because they are closer to Earth.
Stars twinkle because their light always undergoes total internal reflection in the atmosphere.

explanation: Turbulent atmospheric layers continuously change the refractive path of starlight. A star's tiny apparent angular size makes these fluctuations noticeable. A planet's apparent disc averages the effects over many rays, so its twinkling is usually less noticeable. Option C is false because planetary light also undergoes atmospheric refraction.

title: Shining air bubble in water
question: An air bubble is surrounded by water, and light reaches its curved boundary from the water side. An air bubble appears bright against a darker background in water. Which explanation is physically consistent with the water–air interface?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 180" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="8" y="8" width="304" height="164" rx="5" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.18" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" /><circle cx="160" cy="91" r="38" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.6" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M18 91 L122 91 L135 67 L159 54 L184 69 L199 91 L302 91" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M122 91 L112 85 M122 91 L112 97" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><text x="17" y="26" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Water</text><text x="138" y="95" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Air</text><text x="193" y="50" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Bubble surface</text></svg>

options.text: The bubble is bright because its refractive index is higher than that of water.
Every ray striking the bubble must refract into the air, regardless of its angle.
Light is produced inside the bubble by the compression of air.
Some incident rays in water undergo total internal reflection at the water–air boundary because water is optically denser than air.

explanation:
is physically consistent with the water–air interface?

A) The bubble is bright because its refractive index is higher than that of water.

B) Every ray striking the bubble must refract into the air, regardless of its angle.

C) Light is produced inside the bubble by the compression of air.

D) Some incident rays in water undergo total internal reflection at the water–air boundary because water is optically denser than air.

**Correct Answer: D**

**Reason:**

The refractive index of water is higher than that of air. Rays travelling in water can undergo total internal reflection at the bubble boundary when their incidence angle exceeds the water–air critical angle. The reflected rays can make the bubble appear bright. Not every ray is necessarily totally internally reflected.

title: Shining test tube immersed in water
question: A glass test tube containing air is immersed in water; the air–glass–water interfaces can reflect light. A glass test tube containing air is immersed in water and appears bright under suitable illumination. Which statement is the most accurate explanation?

options.text: The test tube appears bright because glass has a refractive index lower than both air and water.
The test tube appears bright because all light entering the tube is absorbed and converted into visible light.
Reflections, including possible total internal reflection at suitable denser-to-rarer interfaces, can direct light towards the observer; the effect depends on the ray angles and refractive indices.
The test tube appears bright because the speed of light is the same in air, glass and water.

explanation:
?

A) The test tube appears bright because glass has a refractive index lower than both air and water.

B) The test tube appears bright because all light entering the tube is absorbed and converted into visible light.

C) Reflections, including possible total internal reflection at suitable denser-to-rarer interfaces, can direct light towards the observer; the effect depends on the ray angles and refractive indices.

D) The test tube appears bright because the speed of light is the same in air, glass and water.

**Correct Answer: C**

**Reason:**

The glass walls and the air–glass–water interfaces produce reflections and refractions. Depending on the direction of incidence, total internal reflection may occur at an interface where light travels from a denser to a rarer medium. Option A reverses the refractive-index relationship and option D ignores the different speeds of light in the media.

title: Interpreting a graph of sin i against sin r
question: The vertical axis is sin i; the horizontal axis is sin r. The straight line passes through the origin. A student plots sin i against sin r for light passing from air into glass. The graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient 1.5. What does the gradient represent?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 220" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M48 22 V181 H294" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none" /><path d="M48 181 L273 34" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M48 181 L273 34" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M48 181 L273 34" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><text x="11" y="20" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">sin i</text><text x="248" y="201" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">sin r</text><text x="150" y="91" font-size="11" fill="#D97706">Straight line</text><text x="52" y="195" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">O</text></svg>

options.text: The refractive index of glass relative to air.
The reciprocal of the refractive index of glass relative to air.
The speed of light in glass divided by the speed of light in air.
The critical angle of glass in degrees.

explanation:
Snell's law gives


n=(sin i / sin r)


The gradient of a graph of sin i against sin r is


(Δ(sin i) / Δ(sin r))=n=1.5


Option B would apply if the axes were interchanged. The gradient is a dimensionless ratio, not an angle.

question: A ray passes through a parallel-sided slab; the path is reversible when the direction of light is reversed. A light ray travels through a rectangular glass slab from air, emerges into air, and then travels back through the same slab in the opposite direction along the emergent path. Which statement is correct under the principle of reversibility of light?

The reverse ray undergoes total internal reflection at the first surface because it is moving towards air.
The reverse ray retraces the original path exactly, including the same lateral displacement in the opposite direction of travel.
The reverse ray emerges perpendicular to the original incident ray because it crosses two interfaces.

explanation: The laws of refraction are reversible. If the direction of a ray is reversed, it retraces the same geometrical path. The lateral displacement has the same magnitude, and the emergent ray remains parallel to the original incident ray. Option B incorrectly assumes that merely travelling towards air guarantees total internal reflection.

question: Medium X Critical angle = 30° Medium Y Critical angle = 45° Both critical angles are measured for the respective media relative to air. Two transparent media, X and Y, have critical angles of 30^° and 45^°, respectively, when surrounded by air. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: Medium Y has the higher refractive index because its critical angle is larger.
Both media have the same refractive index because the refracted ray travels along the interface at the critical angle.
Medium X has a refractive index of 1/sin45^°, while medium Y has a refractive index of 1/sin30^°.
Medium X has the higher refractive index; its refractive index is 2, while that of medium Y is approximately 1.414.

explanation:
For a medium surrounded by air,


n=(1 / sin C)


For X,


n_X=(1 / sin30^°)=2


For Y,


n_Y=(1 / sin45^°)
=sqrt2≈1.414


A smaller critical angle corresponds to a higher refractive index when the surrounding medium is the same.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Detecting a reversed refractive-index ratio
question: A ray travels from glass into air. The angle of incidence is 30^°, and the angle of refraction is 48.6^°. Which expression gives the refractive index of glass relative to air?
diagramSvg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 460 200" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#f8fafc; border-radius:8px; border:1px solid #cbd5e1; font-family:system-ui, sans-serif;">
      <text x="230" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#0f172a">Refraction Through Glass Slab: Lateral Displacement</text>
      <!-- Glass slab -->
      <rect x="100" y="65" width="260" height="70" fill="#e0f2fe" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="1.8"/>
      <text x="330" y="105" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#0369a1">Glass (Dense)</text>
      <!-- Incident Ray -->
      <line x1="60" y1="25" x2="160" y2="65" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>
      <!-- Refracted Ray inside slab (bends towards normal) -->
      <line x1="160" y1="65" x2="220" y2="135" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>
      <!-- Emergent Ray (parallel to incident) -->
      <line x1="220" y1="135" x2="320" y2="175" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>
      <!-- Dotted original path -->
      <line x1="160" y1="65" x2="380" y2="153" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="3,3"/>
      <!-- Lateral displacement line -->
      <line x1="270" y1="155" x2="285" y2="115" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="1.5"/>
      <text x="310" y="140" font-size="9" font-weight="700" fill="#16a34a">Lateral Displacement (d)</text>
      <text x="230" y="190" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#334155">Angle of Incidence i = Angle of Emergence e; Emergent ray is parallel to incident ray</text>
    </svg>

options.text: dfrac{sin48.6^°}{sin30^°}
dfrac{sin30^°}{sin48.6^°}
dfrac{sin30^°}{sin48.6^°}, interpreted as the absolute refractive index of air.
dfrac{sin48.6^°}{sin30^°}, interpreted as the refractive index of air relative to glass.

explanation:
For light travelling from glass to air,


n_{glass relative to air}
=(sin r / sin i)


Thus,


n=(sin48.6^° / sin30^°)
≈(0.75 / 0.5)=1.5


The ratio is reversed compared with the usual air-to-glass form of Snell’s law because the incident medium is now glass. Option B gives the reciprocal, approximately 0.67, which represents air relative to glass.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Refraction through a rectangular glass slab
question: A ray enters a parallel-sided glass slab obliquely. Which statement correctly describes the emergent ray and the lateral displacement?
diagramSvg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 460 200" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#f8fafc; border-radius:8px; border:1px solid #cbd5e1; font-family:system-ui, sans-serif;">
      <text x="230" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#0f172a">Refraction Through Glass Slab: Lateral Displacement</text>
      <!-- Glass slab -->
      <rect x="100" y="65" width="260" height="70" fill="#e0f2fe" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="1.8"/>
      <text x="330" y="105" font-size="10" font-weight="700" fill="#0369a1">Glass (Dense)</text>
      <!-- Incident Ray -->
      <line x1="60" y1="25" x2="160" y2="65" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>
      <!-- Refracted Ray inside slab (bends towards normal) -->
      <line x1="160" y1="65" x2="220" y2="135" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>
      <!-- Emergent Ray (parallel to incident) -->
      <line x1="220" y1="135" x2="320" y2="175" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>
      <!-- Dotted original path -->
      <line x1="160" y1="65" x2="380" y2="153" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="3,3"/>
      <!-- Lateral displacement line -->
      <line x1="270" y1="155" x2="285" y2="115" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="1.5"/>
      <text x="310" y="140" font-size="9" font-weight="700" fill="#16a34a">Lateral Displacement (d)</text>
      <text x="230" y="190" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#334155">Angle of Incidence i = Angle of Emergence e; Emergent ray is parallel to incident ray</text>
    </svg>

options.text: The emergent ray bends towards the normal and has a different direction from the incident ray.
The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, but lateral displacement is always zero.
The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, and the lateral displacement increases if the slab thickness increases while the angle of incidence and refractive index remain fixed.
The emergent ray is perpendicular to the incident ray because the slab has two refracting surfaces.

explanation:
At the first surface, the ray bends towards the normal; at the second, it bends away from the normal. Because the two surfaces are parallel, the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray.

For a slab of thickness t,


d=t(sin(i-r) / cos r)


For fixed i and r, lateral displacement d is proportional to t. Option B is a tempting error: parallel rays need not coincide, and oblique incidence generally produces a non-zero lateral displacement.

question: The diagram shows a coin at a real depth of 12 cm in water of refractive index 4/3. The backward extensions of the refracted rays meet at the apparent image. Which position and apparent shift are correct?
diagramSvg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 460 200" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#f8fafc; border-radius:8px; border:1px solid #cbd5e1; font-family:system-ui, sans-serif;">

      <!-- Refracted Ray inside slab (bends towards normal) -->

      <!-- Dotted original path -->
      <line x1="160" y1="65" x2="380" y2="153" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="3,3"/>
      <!-- Lateral displacement line -->
      <line x1="270" y1="155" x2="285" y2="115" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="1.5"/>
      <text x="310" y="140" font-size="9" font-weight="700" fill="#16a34a">Lateral Displacement (d)</text>
      <text x="230" y="190" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#334155">Angle of Incidence i = Angle of Emergence e; Emergent ray is parallel to incident ray</text>
    </svg>

options.text: Apparent depth 16 cm; apparent shift 4 cm downwards.
Apparent depth 9 cm; apparent shift 3 cm upwards.
Apparent depth 9 cm; apparent shift 3 cm downwards.
Apparent depth 12 cm; apparent shift zero.

explanation:
For near-normal viewing from air into water,


n=(real depth / apparent depth)


Hence,


apparent depth=(12 / 4/3)=9 cm


The apparent shift is


12-9=3 cm


The coin appears raised towards the surface. Option A results from inverting the depth ratio.

question: In the diagram, a ray travels from glass into air and the refracted ray grazes the interface. If the refractive index of glass is 1.5, which interpretation is correct?

      <text x="230" y="190" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#334155">Angle of Incidence i = Angle of Emergence e; Emergent ray is parallel to incident ray</text>
    </svg>

options.text: The angle of refraction is 90^°, and the angle of incidence is also 90^°.
The angle of incidence is 90^°, and the angle of refraction is the critical angle.
The angle of refraction is 0^°, and the angle of incidence is the critical angle.
The angle of refraction is 90^°, and the angle of incidence is the critical angle, approximately 41.8^°.

explanation:
At the critical angle C, the refracted ray travels along the interface, so its angle with the normal is 90^°.


sin C=(1 / 1.5)=frac23



C=sin^{-1}≤ft(frac23right)
≈41.8^°


Option A confuses the grazing refracted ray’s angle with the incident angle. The critical angle is measured inside the denser medium.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Distinguishing critical refraction from total internal reflection
question: A second ray is incident on the same glass–air boundary at 45^°. Which conclusion follows from the figure and the refractive index of glass?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
    <rect x="12" y="94" width="296" height="84" fill="#72B7E8" fill-opacity="0.25"/>
    <path d="M12 94 H308" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/>
    <path d="M160 24 V170" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="5 4" stroke-width="1"/>
    <path d="M86 157 L160 94 L285 94" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none"/>
    <path d="M150 102 L160 94 L147 93" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/>
    <text x="18" y="113" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Glass (n = 1.5)</text>
    <text x="18" y="23" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Air (n = 1)</text>
    <text x="173" y="83" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">r = 90°</text>
    <text x="120" y="140" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">C</text>
    <circle cx="160" cy="94" r="3" fill="#D97706"/>
  </svg>

options.text: The second ray refracts into air at 45^° because the angle is greater than the critical angle.
The second ray undergoes total internal reflection because its angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.
The second ray refracts into air at 90^° because every angle greater than the critical angle produces grazing refraction.
The second ray passes undeviated into air because glass and air have the same boundary normal.

explanation:
The critical angle is


C=sin^{-1}≤ft((1 / 1.5)right)
≈41.8^°


Since 45^°>41.8^°, the ray undergoes total internal reflection. At exactly the critical angle, the refracted ray grazes the interface; above it, no ordinary refracted ray enters the air.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Testing both conditions for total internal reflection
question: Which of the following situations can produce total internal reflection?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 180" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
    <rect x="8" y="88" width="304" height="82" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2"/>
    <path d="M8 88 H312" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/>
    <path d="M160 18 V165" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="4 4"/>
    <path d="M58 147 L160 88 L246 28" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none"/>
    <path d="M160 88 L256 148" stroke="#0D9488" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" stroke-dasharray="5 3"/>
    <text x="15" y="108" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Water</text>
    <text x="15" y="18" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Air</text>
    <text x="167" y="72" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Normal</text>
    <text x="179" y="115" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Possible ray</text>
  </svg>

options.text: Light travels from air into water at 60^°.
Light travels from water into air at an incidence angle of 30^°, when the critical angle is approximately 49^°.
Light travels from glass into water at an angle greater than the critical angle for the glass–water pair.
Light travels from air into glass at an angle of 80^°.

explanation:
Total internal reflection requires both:

1. Light must travel from an optically denser to an optically rarer medium.
2. The angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle for that pair of media.

Only C satisfies both conditions. A and D involve light entering a denser medium, while B has an incidence angle smaller than the critical angle.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Right-angled prism: predicting the ray path
question: A ray enters one of the shorter faces of a right-angled isosceles glass prism normally. The refractive index of glass is 1.5. At the hypotenuse, the angle of incidence is 45^°. What happens?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
    <path d="M55 155 L55 35 L235 155 Z" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/>
    <path d="M15 95 L55 95 L175 95 L175 75" fill="none" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5"/>
    <path d="M55 95 L175 95" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5"/>
    <path d="M175 95 L175 75" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5"/>
    <path d="M168 83 L175 75 L182 83" fill="none" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2"/>
    <text x="12" y="82" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Incident</text>
    <text x="74" y="53" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Glass prism</text>
    <text x="72" y="170" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">45°–45°–90°</text>
  </svg>

options.text: The ray undergoes total internal reflection because 45^° exceeds the critical angle.
The ray emerges through the hypotenuse because every prism face permits refraction.
The ray undergoes total internal reflection only if its angle of incidence is 90^°.
The ray bends towards the normal at the hypotenuse and enters air.

explanation: The critical angle for glass–air is approximately 41.8^°. Since 45^°>41.8^°, total internal reflection occurs at the hypotenuse. The ray is reflected internally, changing its direction by 90^°. Option B ignores the critical-angle condition.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Optical fibre: identifying the role of the core
question: An optical fibre has a core of refractive index 1.50 and cladding of refractive index 1.40. Which statement best explains the ray path shown?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 160" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
    <rect x="15" y="38" width="290" height="84" rx="4" fill="#94A3B8" fill-opacity="0.22" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/>
    <rect x="15" y="53" width="290" height="54" rx="2" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.3" stroke="#2563EB" stroke-width="1"/>
    <path d="M24 80 L75 56 L126 104 L177 56 L228 104 L285 76" fill="none" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5"/>
    <path d="M277 70 L285 76 L275 80" fill="none" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2"/>
    <text x="23" y="29" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Cladding (lower n)</text>
    <text x="24" y="96" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Core (higher n)</text>
  </svg>

options.text: The ray is guided because the core absorbs all the refracted light and re-emits it.
The ray is guided by total internal reflection at the core–cladding interface when the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle for that interface.
The ray is guided because the cladding has a higher refractive index than the core.
The ray is guided because the frequency of light increases at every reflection.

explanation:
The core has the higher refractive index, so light can undergo total internal reflection at the core–cladding interface.


sin C=(1.40 / 1.50)


Thus C≈69^°. For incidence angles inside the core greater than this critical angle, the ray remains guided. Option C reverses the refractive-index relationship.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Why does a diamond sparkle intensely?
question: A diamond has a very high refractive index, approximately 2.42. Which interpretation of the figure is correct?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
    <path d="M160 22 L239 65 L212 147 L160 177 L108 147 L81 65 Z" fill="#A5F3FC" fill-opacity="0.24" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/>
    <path d="M81 65 L239 65 M108 147 L212 147 M160 22 L160 177 M81 65 L160 147 L239 65" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/>
    <path d="M105 48 L160 82 L209 126 L173 151 L133 118 L184 86" fill="none" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5"/>
    <path d="M176 91 L184 86 L183 96" fill="none" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2"/>
    <text x="8" y="17" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Incident light</text>
    <path d="M68 18 L105 48" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/>
    <text x="188" y="171" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Diamond</text>
  </svg>

options.text: The diamond sparkles because light travels faster inside it than in air.
The diamond sparkles because the frequency of light increases at each internal reflection.
The diamond sparkles because every incident ray undergoes total internal reflection, regardless of its angle.
The diamond can sparkle because its small critical angle allows many rays to undergo repeated total internal reflection before emerging.

explanation:
For diamond–air,


C=sin^{-1}≤ft((1 / 2.42)right)
≈24.4^°


This small critical angle makes total internal reflection possible for many internal rays. Suitable facets then direct light towards the observer. Option C is incorrect because rays incident at angles below the critical angle may refract out instead.
